name: Linux Command Line
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Navigate the file system, manage files and permissions, chain commands with pipes, and run processes, SSH and scripts.

lesson.intro: The command line is how developers drive servers, containers, build tools and Git, and on most servers it is the only interface you get. This lesson covers paths, files, permissions, pipes, searching, processes, SSH and your first script.
objectives: Navigate the file system with absolute and relative paths
Create, copy, move and delete files safely, and set permissions with chmod
Combine commands with pipes and redirection, and search with grep and find
Inspect and stop processes, and set environment variables and PATH
Install packages, log in with SSH keys and write a small script

sections.title: The shell and the file system tree
sections.key: Linux keeps everything in one tree under `/`: an absolute path starts with `/` and works anywhere, a relative path starts from where you are.
sections.body:
You log in to a server to find out why a site is down. There is no desktop, just a prompt like `ada@web1:~$`. The program reading your commands is the **shell**, usually **bash** or **zsh**.

Most commands have one shape: name, **options**, **arguments**. In `ls -l /etc`, `-l` is an option and `/etc` the argument; `ls -la` means `ls -l -a`. `man ls` opens the manual (`q` quits).

[[visual]]

An **absolute path** starts with `/`: `/var/log/nginx/error.log`. A **relative path** starts where you are. `.` is the current directory, `..` its parent and `~` your home.

[[visual 2]]

Names are case-sensitive, and names starting with a dot, like `.bashrc`, are hidden from a plain `ls`.

visual.title: The top of the tree

children.label: log/
children.sub: logs: look here when things break

visual.caption: No drive letters: extra disks attach somewhere inside this one tree.

steps.label: Then down into www, then html

sections.pitfall: Confusing `/` (the top of the whole tree) with `~` (your home directory). `cd /` takes you to the very top; `cd ~`, or plain `cd`, takes you home.

check.question: You are in /home/ada/projects. Which path refers to /home/ada/projects/site/index.html?
choices: /site/index.html
../site/index.html
site/index.html
~/site/index.html
check.explanation: A relative path starts from the current directory, so site/index.html is right. /site/... starts at the root of the whole tree, ../site goes up to /home/ada first, and ~/site means /home/ada/site.

sections.title: Moving around: pwd, ls, cd
sections.key: `pwd` says where you are, `ls` shows what is here and `cd` moves you; Tab completion and command history do most of the typing.
sections.body:
The three commands you type most: `pwd` (print working directory: where am I?), `ls` (what is here?) and `cd` (go somewhere else).

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Two habits make you fast. Press **Tab** to complete names, twice to list the choices; if Tab will not complete something, it usually does not exist. Press **Up** for earlier commands, or `Ctrl+R` to search your history.

Get used to silence: a successful command often prints nothing. `cd projects` with no output worked.

visual.title: Moving and looking
rows: Long format: permissions, owner, size, modification time
Includes hidden entries (names starting with a dot), plus `.` and `..`
Long format with sizes like 4.0K and 12M
Sorted by time, newest at the bottom
Up one level; `cd ../..` goes up two
Back to the directory you were in before

sections.code:
ada@web1:~$ pwd
/home/ada
ada@web1:~$ ls -a
.  ..  .bashrc  .ssh  notes.txt  projects
ada@web1:~$ cd projects/site
ada@web1:~/projects/site$ ls -lh
total 12K
drwxr-xr-x 2 ada ada 4.0K Oct 10 images
-rw-r--r-- 1 ada ada 1.2K Oct 14 index.html
-rw-r--r-- 1 ada ada  340 Oct 12 style.css
ada@web1:~/projects/site$ cd -
/home/ada
sections.pitfall: Typing long paths by hand and getting one letter wrong. Let Tab complete them; when Tab refuses, check the spelling or the directory you are in.

activity.title: Find your way around
activity.prompt: Use Tab to complete names, and run pwd whenever you lose track of where you are. Notice which entries appear only with ls -a. The last task previews find, covered in the searching section.

check.question: You are in /var/log/nginx and run `cd ../../..`. Where are you now?
choices: /var
/var/log
/home
check.explanation: Each .. climbs one level: /var/log, then /var, then /. Counting the levels out loud is the reliable way to read a path full of ..

sections.title: Working with files and directories
sections.key: `cp`, `mv` and `rm` act instantly and permanently, and the shell expands wildcards first, so preview a glob with `echo` before giving it to `rm`.
sections.body:
You need to back up a config, make a folder for reports, rename a draft and clear old logs.

[[visual]]

The shell expands **wildcards** (globs) before the command runs: `*` matches any run of characters, `?` exactly one, `[abc]` one listed character. By the time `rm *.tmp` starts it has become `rm a.tmp b.tmp`; rm never sees the star. So `echo *.tmp` previews a glob safely.

[[code]]

There is **no trash can**. `rm` deletes for good, and `cp` and `mv` silently overwrite a file with the same name. Add `-i` to be asked first.

visual.title: Everyday file commands
rows: Creates an empty file, or updates its timestamp
Creates the directory and any missing parents
Moves into a directory, keeping the name
Deletes a file; a directory and everything in it
Prints it all; scrolls and searches (`/word`, `q` quits)
Keeps printing new lines: watch a live log

sections.code:
$ mkdir -p backup/2026
$ cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf backup/2026/
$ cp -r site site-old
$ mv draft.md report.md
$ echo *.log
access.log error.log
$ rm -i *.log
rm: remove regular file 'access.log'? y
rm: remove regular file 'error.log'? y
sections.deeper:
`mv` handles both renaming and moving because a rename is just a move within the same directory.

For quick edits inside a terminal, `nano` is the friendliest editor (its shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the screen); vim is everywhere but takes practice.

In `less`, `G` jumps to the end, `g` to the start, and `n` repeats a search.
sections.pitfall: Running `rm -r` on a glob or path you have not checked. Preview it with `ls` or `echo` first, because a deleted file does not come back.

activity.title: Create, copy and delete
activity.prompt: Predict what each command will print before you run it (often nothing, since silence means success). Before deleting drafts, list its contents so you know exactly what rm -r is about to remove for good.

check.question: What does `mv notes.txt archive/` do when archive is an existing directory?
choices: Moves notes.txt into archive, keeping its name
Renames notes.txt to a file called archive
Copies notes.txt into archive and keeps the original
Fails, because mv can only rename files
check.explanation: When the destination is an existing directory, mv moves the file into it under the same name. mv never leaves the original behind; that would be cp.

sections.title: Permissions and chmod
sections.key: `ls -l` shows read, write and execute for the owner, the group and others; on a directory, x means enter and w means create or delete entries.
sections.body:
You type `./deploy.sh` and get `Permission denied`. The file exists and you own it; its permissions are the problem.

Every file has an **owner**, a **group** and three permission triplets: **u**ser (the owner), **g**roup and **o**thers. Linux applies only the first category that fits you.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

`chmod` takes two notations. **Symbolic** edits bits: `chmod u+x deploy.sh` adds execute for the owner, `chmod go-w notes.txt` removes write from group and others. **Octal** sets everything at once:

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

`chown ada:devs file` changes owner and group and needs **root**. `sudo` runs one command as root.

visual.title: Reading a permission string
visual.caption: The example is `-rwxr-xr--`, as `ls -l` prints it.

visual.title: What each bit allows
rows: Enter it with cd and reach what is inside

visual.title: Working out an octal mode
visual.result: `chmod 640 file`. Common: `755` programs and directories, `644` ordinary files, `600` private files such as SSH keys

sections.code:
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 ada devs 812 Oct 14 deploy.sh
$ ./deploy.sh
bash: ./deploy.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod u+x deploy.sh
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rwxr--r-- 1 ada devs 812 Oct 14 deploy.sh
sections.deeper:
Deleting a file is an operation on the directory, not the file: you need write (and execute) permission on the directory, even if the file itself is read-only and owned by someone else. That is why `/tmp` has the special sticky bit, which limits deletion to each file's owner.

Root skips permission checks entirely, so give `sudo` only to the one command that needs it instead of logging in as root.
sections.pitfall: Fixing a permission error with `chmod 777`. It lets every user on the system change the file; add only the bit that is missing, such as `u+x`.

activity.title: Permission denied
activity.prompt: Read the ls -l output first and predict which scripts you are allowed to run. After the chmod, run ls -l again and find the x that appeared. For secret.txt, work out the octal number before you type it.

check.question: Which command gives a file the permissions rw-r--r--?
choices: chmod 755 file
chmod 644 file
chmod 600 file
chmod 466 file
check.explanation: rw- is 4+2 = 6, and r-- is 4 for both group and others: 644. 755 would add execute everywhere, 600 removes access for group and others, and 466 puts the digits in the wrong triplets.

sections.title: Pipes and redirection
sections.key: A pipe sends one program's output into the next; `>` overwrites a file, `>>` appends, `2>` catches errors, and redirections apply left to right.
sections.body:
Which IP sent the most requests in a 200,000-line access log? No single command knows, but four small ones joined by pipes do.

Every program has three streams: **stdin** (input), **stdout** (output) and **stderr** (errors, kept separate).

[[visual]]

Order matters: in `cmd > all.txt 2>&1`, stdout goes to the file, then stderr follows it. Write `2>&1 > all.txt` and errors still reach the screen.

A **pipe** (`|`) feeds stdout into the next program's stdin:

[[visual 2]]

`uniq` only collapses **adjacent** duplicates, so sort first. Build a pipeline one stage at a time, running it after each `|`.

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Redirection
rows: stdout into the file, replacing what it held

visual.title: Top IPs in an access log

steps.label: `cut -d' ' -f1 access.log`
steps.detail: Keep the first space-separated field: the IP

steps.label: `sort`
steps.detail: Identical IPs end up side by side

steps.label: `uniq -c`
steps.detail: Collapse each run and prefix its count

visual.title: More filters
rows: Saves a copy and passes the text along

sections.code:
$ cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort \
    | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
   4821 203.0.113.7
   1290 198.51.100.23
    877 192.0.2.44

$ grep ERROR app.log > errors.txt
$ wc -l < errors.txt
42
sections.pitfall: Redirecting into the file you are reading, as in `sort data.txt > data.txt`. The shell empties data.txt before sort even starts, so the data is gone.

activity.title: Pipes and filters
activity.prompt: Build each pipeline one stage at a time and run it after every | you add, so you can see the text change at each step. For the visitors, try uniq without sort first and notice why the result is wrong.

check.question: What does `sort names.txt | uniq | wc -l` print?
choices: The total number of lines in names.txt
The most common line in names.txt
The number of distinct lines in names.txt
The number of lines that appear more than once
check.explanation: sort groups identical lines together, uniq keeps one of each group, and wc -l counts what is left: the number of distinct lines.

sections.title: Searching: grep and find
sections.key: `grep` searches inside files for matching lines; `find` searches the tree for files by name, type, size and age. Quote find's patterns.
sections.body:
Two questions come up constantly: which lines mention this? (`grep`) and where is that file? (`find`)

[[visual]]

With no file name, grep reads stdin, so it slots into pipelines: `ps aux | grep nginx`.

[[visual 2]]

Always quote the pattern after `-name`. Unquoted, the shell expands `*.py` against the current folder first, so find receives file names instead of a pattern, or fails.

[[code]]

visual.title: grep pattern file: options
rows: Searches every file under a directory
Prints lines that do **not** match: `grep -v '^#'` hides comments
Counts matching lines instead of printing them
Prints only the names of matching files
Whole words only; extended regex such as `'error|warn'`

visual.title: find tests (combine several)
rows: Names matching the pattern (`-iname` ignores case)
Runs a command on each result: try without it first

sections.code:
$ grep -rn "TODO" src/
src/app.py:14:    # TODO: handle an empty cart
src/utils.py:3:# TODO: remove this helper

$ grep -c ERROR /var/log/app.log
42

$ find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime -1
/var/log/app.log
/var/log/nginx/access.log

$ find ~/Downloads -type f -size +500M
/home/ada/Downloads/ubuntu.iso
sections.pitfall: Leaving the find pattern unquoted. It can appear to work in one folder and fail in another, depending on which files happen to match the glob there.

check.question: Which command lists the files under /etc whose contents mention ssh?
choices: find /etc -name ssh
grep -c ssh /etc
find /etc -type f ssh
grep -rl ssh /etc
check.explanation: grep looks inside files: -r searches the whole tree and -l prints just the matching file names. find -name matches file names, not contents, and grep without -r refuses to read a directory.

sections.title: Processes, environment variables and PATH
sections.key: Every program runs as a process with a PID you can signal; exported environment variables pass settings to programs, and PATH decides which file a command runs.
sections.body:
The server is slow and something is eating the CPU. Every running program is a **process** with a numeric ID, its **PID**.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Processes carry **environment variables**: `HOME`, `USER`, your own `DATABASE_URL`. `echo $HOME` reads one and `env` lists them all. `export API_KEY=abc123` sets a variable *and* hands it to programs you start; without `export`, they cannot see it. Settings vanish when the terminal closes, so put lasting ones in `~/.bashrc`.

**PATH** lists the directories searched, in order, for a command name. `which python3` shows which file runs. Extend it, never replace it: `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`.

visual.title: Finding and stopping processes
rows: Every process: user, PID, CPU, memory, command
Live view sorted by CPU (`q` quits)
Sends **SIGTERM**: a polite request to exit cleanly
Sends **SIGKILL**: enforced at once, no cleanup
Sends **SIGINT** to the foreground program, which usually stops it
Suspends it, then resumes it in the background or foreground

sections.code:
$ ps aux | grep crunch
ada  4821 98.7  2.1 ... python3 crunch.py
$ kill 4821

$ echo $PATH
/home/ada/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
$ which python3
/usr/bin/python3
$ export DATABASE_URL="postgres://db/shop"
sections.deeper:
PATH is a colon-separated list, searched left to right, which is how typing `python3` runs `/usr/bin/python3`. Writing `PATH=~/bin` replaces the whole list, so afterwards even `ls` gives "command not found" until you open a new shell.

`jobs` lists the commands you suspended or started in the background from this shell.

For zsh (the macOS default), lasting settings go in `~/.zshrc` instead of `~/.bashrc`.
sections.pitfall: Reaching for `kill -9` first. SIGKILL gives the program no chance to finish writing files or release locks; try plain `kill` and give it a few seconds.

check.question: You run `export EDITOR=nano` in one terminal, then open a new terminal window. Is EDITOR set there?
choices: No: it lasts only for that shell and the programs started from it
Yes: export saves the variable permanently
Yes, but only for programs run with sudo
No: export only works inside shell scripts
check.explanation: export passes a variable down to child processes of that shell, nothing more. A new window starts a fresh shell, so to make it permanent you add the export line to ~/.bashrc.

sections.title: Packages, SSH and shell scripts
sections.key: Install software with the package manager, log in to servers with an SSH key pair, and save repeated commands as a script that stops at the first failure.
sections.body:
Three skills turn you from a visitor into someone who can run a server.

[[visual]]

**SSH** gives you an encrypted shell on another machine: `ssh deploy@203.0.113.10`. Use a key pair instead of a password:

[[visual 2]]

A **shell script** is commands saved in a file, starting with a **shebang** (`#!/usr/bin/env bash`). Make it executable with `chmod +x backup.sh` and run `./backup.sh`.

[[code]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Package managers
rows: `sudo apt update` (refresh the list), `sudo apt install nginx`, `sudo apt upgrade`, `sudo apt remove nginx`
visual.caption: Prefer them to random downloads: dependencies come along, and security fixes arrive with one command.

messages.label: `ssh deploy@srv`
messages.detail: first time: confirm the host key

visual.title: Script essentials
rows: Sets a variable. No spaces around `=`
Uses it, quoted in case it contains spaces
The last exit code: 0 success, anything else failure
Runs b only if a succeeded
Runs b only if a failed
Stops the script at the first failing command

sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Usage: ./backup.sh <directory>
SOURCE="$1"
STAMP=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
NAME="$(basename "$SOURCE")-$STAMP"
DEST="$HOME/backups/$NAME.tar.gz"

mkdir -p "$HOME/backups"
tar -czf "$DEST" "$SOURCE"
echo "Saved $DEST"
sections.deeper:
The first time you connect, ssh shows the server's key fingerprint and stores it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If that key ever changes, ssh warns loudly: it may be a rebuilt server, or someone in the middle.

The private key (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`) never leaves your machine; only the public key (`id_ed25519.pub`) is copied. `scp report.pdf deploy@203.0.113.10:/srv/files/` copies files over the same secure channel.

Without `set -e`, a script carries on after a failed command, often in a broken state: a failed `cd` followed by `rm -r *` deletes the wrong folder.
sections.pitfall: Writing `NAME = value` with spaces. Bash then tries to run a command called NAME with the arguments `=` and `value`, and fails with "command not found".

check.question: What does `cd /srv/app && git pull` do if /srv/app does not exist?
choices: git pull runs in the current directory instead
cd fails, so git pull never runs
The shell creates /srv/app and then pulls
Both commands run, and only the error is hidden
check.explanation: && runs the second command only when the first exits with code 0. That is exactly what you want here: running git pull in the wrong directory could do damage.

keyTerms.definition: The program, such as bash or zsh, that reads your commands, runs them and shows the output.
A path that starts at the root, /, and means the same thing from any directory.
A path interpreted from the current directory; . is here and .. is the parent.
Read, write and execute bits for the owner, the group and others, changed with chmod.
Runs one command as root, the administrator account that bypasses permission checks.
A program's normal output stream (1) and its separate error stream (2).
The | operator, which feeds one command's output into the next command's input.
A running program, identified by a numeric process ID.
A message to a process, such as SIGTERM (please exit), SIGKILL (stop now) or SIGINT (Ctrl+C).
A named string passed to programs; export makes a shell variable visible to them.
The colon-separated list of directories searched, in order, for a command name.
A private key kept on your machine and a public key placed on servers, used to log in without a password.

summary: One tree under `/`: absolute paths start with `/`, relative ones where you are.
Silence means success, Tab completes, and `rm` has no undo: preview first.
Permissions are rwx for user, group and others; on a directory x enters, w creates and deletes.
Pipes chain small tools; `>` overwrites, `>>` appends, `2>` catches errors.
grep searches inside files, find searches for files; quote find patterns.
`kill` asks, `kill -9` forces; `export` passes variables, PATH picks the program.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has only ever used a mouse what happens when you type `grep ERROR app.log | wc -l` and press Enter: how the shell finds the two programs, how text flows between them, and where the final number is printed.

questions.question: What does `mkdir -p reports/2024/q1` do when reports does not exist yet?
choices: Fails because the parent directory reports is missing
Creates one directory literally named reports/2024/q1
Creates reports, then 2024 inside it, then q1 inside that
Creates only q1, in the current directory
questions.explanation: -p creates every missing parent along the path and does not complain if some already exist. Without -p, mkdir fails with "No such file or directory".

questions.question: Type the command that lists the current directory including hidden files, whose names start with a dot.
questions.explanation: Plain ls skips names that start with a dot. -a shows them, including the . and .. entries; -A shows them without . and ..

questions.question: This was meant to copy the site directory into backup. Why did it fail?
questions.code:
cp site backup/
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'site'
choices: backup/ must be created with touch first
cp needs -r to copy a directory and its contents
cp cannot copy into a directory; mv is needed
The source directory needs a trailing slash
questions.explanation: cp copies single files unless you ask for a recursive copy. cp -r site backup/ copies the directory and its contents.

questions.question: You are in /var/www/html. What absolute path does `../../log/nginx` refer to?
choices: /var/www/log/nginx
/log/nginx
/var/www/html/log/nginx
/var/log/nginx
questions.explanation: The first .. goes up to /var/www, the second to /var, and then log/nginx is added: /var/log/nginx.

questions.question: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x---` for backup.sh. Who can run it?
choices: The owner and members of the file's group
Only the owner, and nobody else at all
Every user who can log in to the system
Group members only, but not the owner
questions.explanation: The user triplet rwx and the group triplet r-x both include x. The others triplet --- has nothing, so everyone else cannot run, read or change it.

questions.question: What octal number do you pass to chmod to set `rwxr-xr--`?
questions.explanation: rwx is 4+2+1 = 7, r-x is 4+1 = 5, and r-- is 4. Together: 754.

questions.question: Complete the command so the owner can execute deploy.sh, without changing anyone else's permissions.
choices: +x
u+x
u=x
questions.explanation: u+x adds execute for the owner only. +x adds it for everyone, 777 gives everyone full access, and u=x sets the owner to execute only, removing their read and write.

questions.question: A directory has mode `drw-r--r--`. Its owner, a normal user, tries to `cd` into it. What happens?
choices: It works, because r is enough to enter a directory
It fails: entering a directory needs the x permission
It works, because owners always have full access
It fails, because entering a directory needs the w bit
questions.explanation: On directories, x means "may enter and reach files inside". With rw- the owner has no x, so cd fails with Permission denied. Owners get no automatic bypass; only root does.

questions.question: missing.txt does not exist. What ends up in out.txt after `ls missing.txt 2>&1 > out.txt`?
choices: The error message, since 2>&1 sends it to the file
The error message twice, once per redirection
The literal text 2>&1 followed by the error
Nothing; the error still appears in the terminal
questions.explanation: Redirections run left to right. 2>&1 points stderr at wherever stdout points at that moment, the terminal. Then > moves only stdout to the file. Write ls missing.txt > out.txt 2>&1 to capture both.

questions.question: Complete the pipeline so it prints the most common line in names.txt together with its count.
choices: uniq -c
wc -l
uniq
grep -c
questions.explanation: After sorting, identical lines sit together, and uniq -c collapses each group into one line prefixed with its count. sort -rn then puts the biggest count first. Plain uniq would drop the counts.

questions.question: A script runs this line every hour. Complete it so each run adds the date to the end of log.txt instead of replacing the file.
questions.explanation: >> appends to the file. > would truncate it every hour, leaving only the latest date. | expects a command, not a file, and 2> redirects only errors.

questions.question: What does `grep -c error app.log` print?
choices: The total number of times error appears
Every line containing error, with line numbers
The number of lines that contain error
The names of the files that contain error
questions.explanation: -c counts matching lines, so a line with "error" twice still counts once. -n would print the lines with numbers, and -l would print file names.

questions.question: Type a find command that lists everything under the current directory whose name ends in `.py`.
questions.explanation: find starts at . (the current directory) and -name tests each file name against the pattern. The quotes stop the shell from expanding *.py before find sees it.

questions.question: This command fails when run in a directory that contains a.txt and b.txt. Why?
questions.code:
find docs -name *.txt
find: paths must precede expression: `b.txt'
choices: The shell expanded *.txt before find ran; quote it
find cannot search inside a directory named docs
-name only accepts exact file names, not patterns
find needs -type f before -name to work
questions.explanation: The shell replaced *.txt with a.txt b.txt, so find received "-name a.txt b.txt" and choked on the extra word. Writing -name "*.txt" passes the pattern through to find.

questions.question: What does `kill 4821` do?
choices: Sends SIGKILL, which ends the process instantly
Pauses the process until you resume it with fg
Deletes the program file that process 4821 runs
Sends SIGTERM, asking the process to exit cleanly
questions.explanation: With no signal given, kill sends SIGTERM (15), which a program can catch to save its work and exit. SIGKILL needs kill -9 and cannot be caught.

questions.question: After the first line, every command fails. What went wrong?
questions.code:
PATH=~/bin
ls
bash: ls: command not found
choices: ~/bin must be created with mkdir -p first
PATH must be written in lowercase as path
PATH was replaced, not extended; use PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
ls is built into the shell and cannot be found through PATH
questions.explanation: The assignment threw away /usr/bin and /bin, so the shell no longer finds ls. Prepending keeps the old list: PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH".

questions.question: You set `API_KEY=abc123` in your shell, but a script you run cannot see it. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.answer: A plain assignment creates a shell variable that only the current shell can see. Run `export API_KEY` (or `export API_KEY=abc123`) so programs started from the shell inherit it.
questions.explanation: Child processes receive only exported variables. You can also set a variable for one command: API_KEY=abc123 ./script.sh.

questions.question: Match each directory to what it normally holds.

pairs.right: Log files from the system and services
Installed programs such as ls and grep
Scratch files that may vanish on reboot

questions.explanation: These conventions hold on almost every Linux system, so knowing them tells you where to look: config in /etc, logs in /var/log, programs in /usr/bin and your own work under /home.

questions.question: Your home directory is /home/ada and you are in /home/ada/projects. Which paths refer to /home/ada/notes.txt? Select all that apply.
choices: ~/notes.txt
../notes.txt
/home/ada/notes.txt
./notes.txt
/notes.txt
questions.explanation: ~ expands to /home/ada, .. climbs from projects to /home/ada, and the absolute path is the same file spelled out. ./notes.txt would be inside projects, and /notes.txt sits at the root of the tree.

questions.question: You are in /etc/nginx, run `cd /var/log`, then run `cd -`. Where are you now?
choices: /var
/home/ada
/etc/nginx
questions.explanation: cd - returns to the previous directory (bash keeps it in OLDPWD) and prints its path. Running cd - again would take you back to /var/log.

questions.question: A folder holds a.txt, b.txt and notes.md. You run `ls *.txt`. What does the ls program actually receive as arguments?
choices: The single argument *.txt, which ls expands itself
The two arguments a.txt and b.txt
Every file name in the folder, which ls then filters
Nothing; ls reads the pattern from standard input
questions.explanation: The shell expands the glob before starting the program, so ls just sees a list of names. This is why echo *.txt previews a glob safely, and why find patterns need quotes. (If nothing matches, bash passes the pattern through unchanged.)

questions.question: Type the command that prints the end of /var/log/app.log and keeps printing new lines as they are written.
questions.explanation: tail shows the last lines of a file, and -f (follow) keeps the file open and prints new lines as they arrive. Press Ctrl+C to stop watching.

questions.question: Match each octal digit to the permissions it sets within one triplet.
questions.explanation: Add r = 4, w = 2 and x = 1: 4+2+1 = 7, 4+2 = 6, 4+1 = 5, 4 alone is read only and 0 is nothing.

questions.question: Type the command that makes secret.txt readable and writable by its owner only, with no access at all for group and others.
questions.explanation: 6 (rw-) for the owner, 0 (---) for group and for others. SSH refuses to use a private key whose permissions are looser than this.

questions.question: The directory /shared is `drwxrwxr-x root team`. Inside it, report.txt is `-rw-r--r-- alice team`. Bob is in the team group. What happens when Bob runs `rm -f /shared/report.txt`?
choices: It fails: Bob has no write permission on report.txt
It fails: only root can delete another user's file
It works: deleting needs write permission on the directory, which Bob has
It works, but only because -f overrides every permission check
questions.explanation: Deleting removes an entry from the directory, so the directory's w and x bits decide, not the file's. The group triplet rwx lets Bob do it. -f only skips the confirmation prompt. Shared folders like /tmp set the sticky bit (drwxrwxrwt) to stop exactly this.

questions.question: What changes when you add `2> /dev/null` to `find / -name passwd`?
choices: Error messages such as Permission denied are discarded, and results still print
The results are discarded, and only error messages print
Both results and errors are saved to a file called null
find runs as root, so no Permission denied errors occur
questions.explanation: 2> redirects only stream 2, stderr, and /dev/null swallows whatever is written to it. The matches travel on stdout, so they still reach your screen.

questions.question: What line does this pipeline print? Ignore leading spaces.
questions.explanation: sort gives a, b, b, b, c. uniq -c turns that into "1 a", "3 b", "1 c". sort -rn puts the largest count first, and head -n 1 keeps only that line: 3 b.

questions.question: Type a grep command that searches every file under src/ for TODO and shows line numbers.
questions.explanation: -r searches the directory tree recursively and -n prefixes each match with its line number, so the output reads file:line:text.

questions.question: What does `grep -v '^#' app.conf` print?
choices: Only the lines that start with #
The number of comment lines in app.conf
Every line, with the # characters removed
Every line that does not start with #
questions.explanation: -v inverts the match, and ^# means "# at the start of the line". Together they hide comment lines, a quick way to read just the active settings of a config file.

questions.question: A script is stuck in an infinite loop in your terminal. What is the usual way to stop it?
choices: Press Ctrl+C, which sends SIGINT to the foreground program
Press Ctrl+Z, which ends the program and frees its memory
Press Ctrl+D, which sends SIGKILL to the program
Type kill at the prompt while the loop keeps running
questions.explanation: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, which stops most programs. Ctrl+Z only suspends the program (it stays in memory until resumed or killed), and Ctrl+D signals end of input, which a loop ignores.

questions.question: Type the command that shows the full path of the program that runs when you type python3.
questions.explanation: which searches PATH the same way the shell does and prints the first match, such as /usr/bin/python3. It is the quickest way to debug "wrong version" problems.

questions.question: On Ubuntu, type the command that installs the package tree, with administrator rights.
questions.explanation: apt is the package manager on Debian and Ubuntu, and installing system software needs root, hence sudo. Run sudo apt update first if the package list is old.

questions.question: You want to log in to deploy@203.0.113.10 without typing a password each time. What is the right setup?
choices: Copy your private key into the server's authorized_keys file
Save the password in ~/.bashrc as SSH_PASSWORD
Create a key pair with ssh-keygen and put the public key on the server
Run ssh with sudo so the server skips the password
questions.explanation: The public key goes on the server (ssh-copy-id appends it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys) and the private key never leaves your machine. Copying the private key anywhere defeats the point, and a saved password in a file is easy to steal.

questions.question: This script prints an error and then ", Ada". What is the bug?
questions.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
greeting = "Hello"
echo "$greeting, $1"

$ ./greet.sh Ada
./greet.sh: line 2: greeting: command not found
, Ada
choices: Variables must be declared with var before they are used
The spaces around = make bash run greeting as a command
$1 is empty because arguments need -- in front of them
The shebang must be #!/bin/sh for echo to work
questions.explanation: In bash, NAME=value must have no spaces. With spaces, bash runs a command called greeting with the arguments = and "Hello", which fails, so $greeting stays empty. Write greeting="Hello".
